newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Menem insists on hopes for Falklands if Labour wins.
newsitem.headline: Menem insists on hopes for Falklands if Labour wins.

text.p: Argentine President Carlos Menem said on Thursday he hoped Britain would change its policy on the Falklands if Labour wins the May 1 election.

The Peronist president, who periodically promises his country he will win back the South Atlantic islands by 2000, told Brazilian correspondents: "We are going to continue with the same policies. But I hope that England doesn't carry on with the same policy under a new government, if Labour wins."
His comments were reported by the local media on Thursday.

Britain and Argentina fought a 10-week war over the archipelago in 1982. Argentina lost the war but maintains its claim to the sparsely populated islands it calls the Malvinas, saying they were "usurped" by Britain in 1833.

The two countries have restored diplomatic relations and forged close trade links, signing a cooperation deal on oil exploration in Falklands waters in 1995. But Britain refuses to discuss the issue of sovereignty and rejects Menem's talk of shared sovereignty, while islanders are unimpressed with Argentina's "charm offensive" intended to win their trust.

The Labour Party this week denied a statement by Argentine Defence Minister Jorge Dominguez to Jane's Defence Weekly that Labour, tipped to win the election, would take a softer stance on Falklands sovereignty.

A party statement said there was "not a shred of truth in the suggestion that there might be any change of policy towards the Falklands were Labour to be elected on May 1." Labour also denied that party leader Tony Blair, widely expected to be the next British prime minister, had had meetings with Argentine Foreign Minister Guido Di Tella.

Foreign diplomats say Argentina has convinced Britain and the islanders that it is now a modern democracy, nothing like the brutal military dictatorship that launched the war, in which 1,000 Argentine and British soldiers lost their lives.

Menem vowed Argentina would "never again resort to that damned war that caused Argentine huge harm." But he insisted that "in the year 2000 the Argentine flag could fly in the islands that belong to us, sharing sovereignty or not."
"The English know very well the islands are Argentine, because there is documentation of the usurpation of 1833 in Britain's Foreign Ministry," the Peronist president said.
